extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house counsel, law firms, and Lex Machina subscribers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and metrics for analyzing patent litigation (district trends, timing, PTAB/IPR flow, findings, damages, judges, parties, and law firm activity) to support strategy, budgeting, and venue/ counsel selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of winning a motion to stay pending PTAB
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering the expense of filing a motion to stay pending PTAB, companies and litigators should know the likelihood of winning the motion - which turns out to differ depending on the district.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant rates for motions to stay pending PTAB decided in 2015 and 2016: Eastern District of Texas, District of Delaware, and Northern District of California had similar grant rates of 55-60%; Central District of California denied motions to stay pending PTAB at a higher rate. Timing to decide also varies (e.g., Northern District of California is slower to decide than Central District of California). Use district-specific grant rates and decision timing when budgeting and deciding whether to file a stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design vs. utility patent litigation concentration and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Although comprising a smaller fraction of litigated patents, design patent litigation is far more consistent than utility patent litigation and remains highly concentrated in particular districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patent litigation is highly concentrated in the Central District of California (which saw a 4.8% increase over 2015), with the Southern District of New York a distant second (4.3% increase). Use concentration metrics by district and year-to-year percent change to evaluate venue risk and case distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: ANDA litigation volume and district concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Track new ANDA cases by year/month to understand trends in Hatch-Waxman litigation and identify district concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ANDA cases rose sharply in 2014-2015, declined in 2016 to 2010-2011 levels. ANDA litigation is heavily concentrated in the District of New Jersey and District of Delaware; these districts have had significantly more cases filed than districts below the top ten. Use temporal charts (year/month) and top-district counts/percentage changes for planning and practice-focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge caseloads and impact on decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Top judges by new cases, assignments, and case outcomes reveal where patent litigation is busiest and how individual judges' caseloads affect findings and summary judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Judge Gilstrap (E.D.Tex.) had 1,119 cases in 2016, topping charts for cases reaching findings and summary judgments; Judge Andrews (D.Del.) was second. Use judge-level metrics (cases assigned, cases with findings, summary judgments) to assess likely timeline and decision patterns, keeping in mind local assignment orders (e.g., general orders assigning high percentages to single judges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Party-level concentration and plaintiff/defendant profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify top plaintiffs and defendants, whether they are patent monetization entities (PMEs) or operating companies, and the primary districts where they litigate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top plaintiffs in 2016 were mostly PMEs; Whirlpool was an exception (ranked 15th). Samsung was the top defendant (37 cases). Each party is shown with the district where the majority of their cases appear and percent of the party's cases in that court—use these metrics to evaluate opponent behavior, venue preferences, and concentration risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law firm activity and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure law firms by number of plaintiff- and defendant-side cases and distinguish national firms from regionally concentrated firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Russ, August & Kabat (110 plaintiff cases in 2016); Fish & Richardson (160 defendant cases). Lex Machina classifies firms as 'national' vs. district-focused (Delaware/Texas). Use firm-level case counts and client lists to benchmark outside counsel and to compare proposed budgets/timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping of patent findings to procedural methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent findings (infringement, non-infringement, invalidity, unenforceability) tend to be reached by particular procedural mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings of infringement tend to come from trial or consent/default judgment; findings of non-infringement or invalidity are more likely to come from summary judgment. Use procedure-to-finding mappings to prioritize motions or settlement strategies depending on desired outcome and likely procedural path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Alice on §101 invalidations
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Alice (June 19, 2014) trends show increased invalidations under 35 U.S.C. § 101, particularly for computer-implemented inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidations under §101 rose to record levels after Alice; §101 invalidation counts swung by quarter in 2015 and declined steadily in 2016. Track quarterly §101 invalidation counts and district distribution when assessing subject-matter risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity basis categorization and trend tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity findings are categorized by legal basis (e.g., 101 subject matter, 102 anticipation/novelty, 103 obviousness, 112 definiteness/written description/enablement, other) and should be tracked over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charts show the number of patents invalidated by basis per quarter (2013-2016). Use basis-level trends to identify predominant grounds for invalidation in given timeframes and districts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Districts with most §101 invalidations
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify top districts by cases with patents invalidated under 35 U.S.C. §101 (for lack of patentable subject matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For cases filed 2012-2016 with invalidity finding in 2016, top districts included D.Del., C.D.Cal., N.D.Ill., E.D.Tex., S.D.Cal., etc., with counts (e.g., D.Del. 8 cases). Use district-specific invalidation frequencies when selecting venue or evaluating subject-matter risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using boxplots to understand timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Boxplots summarize distributions of event timing using median, upper/lower quartiles, and whiskers; interpreting these elements helps with strategy, budgeting, and scheduling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key observations: Median splits data 50/50. Box bounds enclose middle 50% (25th to 75th percentile). A compressed box indicates consistent timing; an elongated box indicates spread/outliers. Whiskers show outside bounds; statistical convention flags outliers beyond 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR). Use boxplots to assess likely timing ranges and probability of early vs late events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Median timing metrics for injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Median times to key remedies/events provide a usable single-number expectation for planning and budgeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example medians: preliminary injunction median = 3.8 months (box bounds 2.0–13.5 months); permanent injunction median = 11.6 months (box bounds 5.4–23.8 months). Note where the median lies within box bounds to infer skew; the median closer to one edge indicates asymmetry. Use median and quartiles for fee arrangements, scheduling, and client expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case resolution categorization and rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify case terminations into resolution types (likely settlement, procedural outcomes, claimant win, claim defendant win) and track proportions over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For cases terminating 2009-2016: 74.6% settled, 15.3% procedural outcomes, 6.1% claimant wins, 4.0% claim defendant wins. For 2016 terminations alone: 76.7% settled, 13.8% procedural, 5.5% claimant win, 4.0% claim defendant win. Use resolution mix to inform settlement likelihood and expected end-state distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages frequency, distribution, and skew
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze frequency of compensatory damages awards and the skewed distribution of award amounts (many small awards, few large outliers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensatory damages awarded in ~1.8% of terminated cases (since 2000). Distribution is highly skewed: 90% of total compensatory awards are under $9.6M; 75% under $1.7M; median approx $170,000. Juries have awarded about seven times more in total than judges ($15B vs $1.9B). Use percentiles (25th, median, 75th, 90th, max) to model exposure and to set expectations for damages budgeting and settlement negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: District-level generosity in damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare median compensatory damages per case across districts to identify jurisdictions that award higher damages relative to case volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative to cases filed, E.D.Tex. and S.D.Cal. were most generous; M.D.Fla. and E.D.Mich. least generous. Median compensatory damages per case: e.g., D.Del. $16.29M (43 cases with damages), E.D.Tex. $7.37M (111 cases). Use district medians and case counts when assessing venue risk and expected damages exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages allocation by judgment type
rubrics_metrics.description: Total damages awarded are distributed by judgment type (consent judgment, default judgment, judge, jury trial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 2000-2016 totals: jury trials accounted for ~78.4% of damages ($17.8B across 413 cases), consent judgments ~7.9% ($1.787B across 208 cases), judge decisions and default judgments comprised other shares. Include costs and attorneys' fees where applicable. Use judgment-type allocation to estimate likely damages magnitude given expected resolution path.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB (IPR/CBM) petition volume and trial flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Track IPR and CBM petitions filed over time and the flow of petitions through institution, settlement, termination, and final written decisions to assess likelihoods of different outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR activity declined slightly in 2015 but remained similar to 2014. Lex Machina's trial flow diagram shows flow from petition filing through final written decision, including settlement and procedural outcomes—use flow probabilities to evaluate petition strategies and expected terminal outcomes. Also track monthly petition counts and trial-type splits (IPR vs CBM).

rubrics_metrics.name: ITC investigation volume and dispositive outcomes by ALJ
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor ITC investigations filed by year and the dispositive outcomes (e.g., cease & desist order, general exclusion order, no violation) by ALJ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charts show ITC investigations filed 2007-2015 and dispositive outcomes by current ALJ for investigations noticed and terminating 2007-2015. Use ALJ-level and outcome-level data to anticipate ITC resolution likelihoods and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of median and boxplot interpretations for strategic decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ medians and boxplot shapes (compression/elongation, whisker length) to form expectations about timing, budgeting, and scheduling for cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The median is a robust average for expected timing. A compressed box indicates consistency (more predictable timing), while an elongated box suggests long tail risk. Whiskers define reasonable bounds; extreme outliers beyond 1.5*IQR should be treated as exceptional. Apply these interpretations when setting flat fees, estimating resource allocation, and planning trials.
